current_criteria.name: avoidance_of_ambiguous_visual_references
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer uses unambiguous visual anchors — such as specific object identifiers (e.g., ‘the red car with the blue stripe’, ‘the person holding the sign’) — to refer to a single, visually distinct element in the image. It penalizes only when the reference could reasonably apply to multiple or indistinct visual elements — e.g., ‘a red thing’, ‘the object on the left’, or ‘something in the background’. This criterion is ONLY applicable when: (1) the question explicitly demands precise visual identification of a single, specific object or instance (e.g., ‘identify the object’, ‘what is this?’, ‘which one?’, ‘point to the X’), and (2) the visual context contains multiple visually similar or indistinct elements. Ambiguity is penalized only if the answer is otherwise factually correct — and never for vague phrasing in contextually unambiguous settings (e.g., ‘a red chair’ when only one red chair exists). This criterion is NOT applicable to: (1) subjective, interpretive, aesthetic, or narrative questions (e.g., ‘what is the mood?’), (2) binary, presence/absence, or yes/no questions, (3) questions asking for general descriptions of background, lighting, or decor (e.g., ‘dark brown background’), (4) compositional or structural analysis where broad terms are appropriate, (5) questions that do not demand precise visual identification of a single, specific instance, (6) any answer containing hallucinations or factual errors — which must be disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image first, (7) questions asking for inferred user activity, software function, or non-visible states — even if visually grounded — which are evaluated under other criteria, (8) questions asking for animal type, species, or general classification — which are not specific instance identification, (9) questions about linguistic terms, usage, or semantic conventions — even if visually anchored — which are evaluated under other criteria, and (10) questions that do not require identifying a single, specific visual element — including questions about counts, general presence, or contextual reasoning — even if multiple objects are present. This criterion is NOT a tiebreaker — it is a refinement metric for factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must be skipped entirely if the answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded. Workers must evaluate whether the reference could reasonably refer to more than one visual element — not whether the phrasing is technically precise or descriptive — and must prioritize visual uniqueness over linguistic specificity. This criterion does NOT penalize contextually grounded inferences or visually supported interpretations — only lack of unique visual anchors — and must not override factual accuracy or visual grounding. It is not a tool to penalize vague or ambiguous phrasing — only to penalize ambiguity in factually correct answers — and must not be used to resolve ties between hallucinated or factually incorrect answers — which must be disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image first. Workers must verify that the answer is factually correct and visually grounded before applying this criterion — and must disqualify any answer that fails these — even if the reference appears ambiguous or imprecise. The criterion must be applied only after factual_consistency_with_the_image has been confirmed — and must be skipped if the answer is hallucinated, misidentified, or factually incorrect. It is not applicable to questions that do not require identifying a single, specific visual element — including questions about counts, general presence, or contextual reasoning — and must not be applied to interpretive or compositional questions. The criterion should not be used to penalize descriptive, inventory-style, or detailed description questions — which are the most common in visual QA — to avoid penalizing accurate, specific answers. Workers must not use this criterion to evaluate visual clarity, detail level, or relative prominence — which are not forms of ambiguity — and must only penalize cases where a term like ‘the object on the left’ or ‘a red thing’ could reasonably refer to multiple or indistinct visual elements — not when a visual element is described as ‘vague’ or ‘blurry’. The criterion must also explicitly exclude any evaluation of which term is ‘more accurate’ or ‘more descriptive’ — and must not be used to resolve ties based on linguistic detail. It should also clarify that ‘ambiguity’ refers to referential ambiguity — not perceptual vagueness — and must include a clear example of when a vague description is acceptable (e.g., describing a blurry object as ‘vague’) versus when it is ambiguous (e.g., ‘the red thing’ referring to multiple red objects). Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that it is inapplicable to any answer that contains hallucinations or misrepresentations — and must clearly define that ‘visual reference’ must refer to visually present, non-hallucinated elements. It should also emphasize that ambiguity is penalized only when the answer is factually correct — and that generic terms like ‘the person in the background’ are acceptable if they refer to a single, visually identifiable individual — not if they refer to multiple or indistinct individuals. Additionally, the criterion must emphasize that it does not evaluate inferred actions or non-visible objects — and must explicitly state that any answer containing hallucinated visual details is disqualified under ‘factual_consistency_with_the_image’ — and should not be evaluated under this criterion. The criterion must also clarify that it is not a tiebreaker — and should be skipped entirely if the answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy over linguistic clarity — and that ambiguous or vague phrasing is only penalized if the answer is factually correct. When visual evidence is clear and unambiguous, the answer must reflect that precision — even if it includes terms like ‘two wooden benches’ or ‘two wooden walls’ — as long as those claims are visually supported. The criterion should not allow for a trade-off between factual accuracy and linguistic clarity — and should explicitly state that any answer with factual errors is disqualified regardless of its clarity or specificity. Finally, it should include a warning that workers must prioritize visual fidelity over linguistic precision — even if the latter appears more ‘clean’ or ‘well-phrased’. This criterion is explicitly gated by factual_consistency_with_the_image — and any answer that fails this gatekeeper is disqualified from all other criteria — including this one — and must not be evaluated under this criterion — even if it appears to be a 'tiebreaker' for visual reference ambiguity. The criterion is strictly for refining factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must not be used to evaluate or compare hallucinated or factually incorrect answers — even if they appear more specific or visually grounded. The description must also explicitly state that the criterion is only a refinement metric — not a gatekeeper — and that any claim of ambiguity or vagueness in such answers must be evaluated after verifying factual accuracy. The description must also clarify that 'ambiguity' refers to referential ambiguity — not semantic inaccuracy — and must include examples of when a term is semantically correct but visually ambiguous — versus when it is semantically incorrect — which the current description fails to address. The criterion must also be explicitly excluded from evaluation for answers that misrepresent visual evidence — even if they use unambiguous terms — because the criterion is only for factually correct, visually grounded answers — not for factually incorrect ones. The worker agent's thought process demonstrates a failure to prioritize factual accuracy — and the criterion must be explicitly tied to visual grounding and factual consistency as prerequisites — with no exceptions for linguistic precision. The description must also clarify that the criterion is not a tool to penalize vague phrasing — only to penalize ambiguity in factually correct answers — and must not be used to resolve ties between hallucinated or factually incorrect answers. Finally, the criterion must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for answers that are factually incorrect — even if they use unambiguous or precise language — because the criterion is only for factually correct, visually grounded answers — not for factually incorrect ones.

current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer includes all semantically required visual elements necessary to fulfill the question’s literal, measurable visual inventory demand — and only when the question explicitly demands an exhaustive, measurable, and literal visual enumeration (e.g., ‘list all objects’, ‘what is on the table?’, ‘describe composition’, ‘what is the text?’). It is inapplicable to: (1) binary, yes/no, or single-attribute questions (e.g., ‘Is this a red car?’), (2) interpretive, inferential, or contextual questions (e.g., ‘What is the mood?’, ‘What is the object doing?’, ‘Describe the style’), (3) questions requiring inferred action, behavior, or state — even if visual objects are present — because those are not inventory-style, (4) aesthetic or compositional questions asking about framing, contrast, or structure — unless explicitly demanding a literal visual inventory (e.g., ‘list all foreground/background elements’), (5) questions where visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — in which case the answer must reflect calibrated uncertainty or question relevance, and (6) any question that does not explicitly demand an exhaustive, individualized visual inventory (e.g., general, representative, or averaged descriptions). Completeness is only a tiebreaker metric — and only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — comparing which answer includes all semantically required visual elements (e.g., visible objects, text, logos, spatial relationships, compositional framing) without omission. It does not penalize inclusion of contextually relevant, visually verifiable details (e.g., background objects, peripheral notes) — only omission of elements that are semantically required to fulfill the question’s literal intent. ‘Semantically required’ means elements directly necessary to answer the question’s core visual inventory demand — e.g., for ‘What is on the table?’, completeness requires listing all visible items on the table — not every object in the room; for ‘Describe the composition’, completeness requires including foreground/background, relative positioning, and compositional framing — even if not the primary subject; for ‘What is the text?’, completeness requires including all visible text — even if not directly referenced — if it is visually present and semantically relevant to the question. Completeness does not reward verbosity — but penalizes omission of semantically required elements — even if the answer includes non-essential commentary. It is not a standalone metric — and should never override factual accuracy or visual grounding. Workers must evaluate only visually verifiable elements — not inferential or conceptual interpretations — and must reject any answer that misrepresents visual evidence — even if it appears thorough. When visual evidence is ambiguous, completeness is not evaluated — and workers must mark the answer as uncertain. Examples of applicability: ‘What is on the table?’ → list all visible items on the table; ‘What is the color of the text?’ → include all visible text colors; ‘Describe the composition’ → include foreground/background, spatial relationships, and framing. Examples of inapplicability: ‘What is the mood?’ → interpretive, not visual inventory; ‘What is the object doing?’ → inferential, not direct visual inventory; ‘Is this a red car?’ → binary, not multi-element; ‘What is the object’s function?’ → inferential, not visual. Completeness must be evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and if an answer contains a factual error, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of coverage. Workers must not use completeness to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must prioritize factual coverage over stylistic minimalism. Completeness is not applicable to questions where the answer is a single factual claim — even if it involves inference — and must be evaluated only for multi-element, inventory-style questions with clear, unambiguous visual evidence. Workers must not apply completeness to hallucinated or visually unsupported claims — even if plausible — and must not penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — only for omission of semantically required elements. The criterion is not a tool to resolve ties between visually incorrect or hallucinated answers — only between factually correct, visually grounded answers. The description must unambiguously exclude any question type not meeting the above criteria — including subjective, inferential, or ambiguous questions — and must explicitly state that completeness is only a tiebreaker for inventory-style questions with clear visual evidence. Workers must not assume that all visible visual elements are ‘semantically relevant’ — only those directly required to answer the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also avoid penalizing factual, verifiable details that are visually present and directly relevant to the question’s literal intent — even if they are not the ‘primary’ answer. The description must clearly state that for binary classification or posture-based questions, the visual distinction (e.g., ‘legs bent’) is semantically required — and that omission of such a detail, even if not the ‘main point’, reduces completeness. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that ‘unnecessary detail’ refers to non-essential, contextually irrelevant information — not factual, visually verifiable details that are critical to answering the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also explicitly state that completeness does not apply to questions requiring inferred action, behavior, or state — even if visual objects are present — because those are not inventory-style. It must also clarify that 'semantically required' elements are those necessary to fulfill the question’s literal, measurable, or compositional intent — not speculative or exaggerated claims about dominance, proportion, or scale. It must also prohibit penalizing answers for omitting such claims if they are visually ambiguous or not essential to the question’s intent — and must explicitly exclude compositional or relational questions from being evaluated under completeness unless they demand explicit, verifiable quantitative or spatial comparisons. Additionally, the criterion should explicitly warn workers not to confuse completeness with precision or verbosity — and to avoid penalizing factually correct answers for being less detailed — especially when the added detail is unsupported or misleading. The criterion must be applied only when the question explicitly demands a multi-element, inventory-style visual description — and must not be applied to open-ended, detail-rich, or subjective questions. It must also clarify that completeness rewards inclusion of semantically required visual elements — not any visible details — and must penalize omission of those elements — even if the answer includes other non-essential details. The criterion must also explicitly exclude questions that are not inventory-style — and must require that the question’s intent be unambiguous — to avoid misapplication. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that completeness is not a tiebreaker — and must not be used to penalize answers for being less detailed — only for omitting semantically required elements. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy — and completeness is only a tiebreaker for factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must not be applied to factually incorrect answers — even if they appear more complete.

current_criteria.name: consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer’s non-literal inferences — such as inferred activity, contextual function, material behavior, or artistic intent — are logically coherent with real-world domain knowledge, but ONLY when those inferences are minimally speculative and directly supported by verifiable visual evidence (e.g., visible interface, brand, object type, posture, or environmental context). It is inapplicable to: (1) literal visual claims (e.g., object identity, color, position, count, or attribute state), which are evaluated under visual grounding and factual consistency; (2) aesthetic, interpretive, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘composition’, ‘style’, ‘visual harmony’), which are evaluated under other criteria; (3) visual inventories (e.g., ‘list all objects’), which are evaluated under completeness; (4) questions demanding precise numerical or positional answers, which are evaluated under specificity; (5) questions where visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded — in such cases, workers must defer to clarity, specificity, or uncertainty markers — and must not apply this criterion. This criterion is ONLY invoked AFTER visual fidelity and factual correctness are confirmed — any answer with visual hallucinations or misrepresentations is disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image and cannot be assessed here. It is a tiebreaker metric ONLY when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and only for non-hallucinatory, minimally speculative inferences that are contextually supported by verifiable visual content (e.g., ‘the person is likely browsing Apple-related pages’ based on visible screen content — not fabricating non-visible details like ‘the person is wearing a jersey’). Hallucinations (inventing visual content not present in the image) are always disqualifying — even if plausible — and must be penalized under factual_consistency_with_the_image. Domain knowledge alignment is NOT a substitute for visual fidelity — it cannot override or validate visually unsupported claims. The criterion does NOT penalize plausible inferences grounded in visual context — even if not explicitly stated — as long as they are not hallucinations. It also does NOT evaluate aesthetic or subjective interpretations — those are not domain knowledge claims. If a claim is visually supported and domain-plausible, it is preferred — but if it is visually incorrect, it is disqualified regardless of plausibility. The criterion should not be used to resolve ties when one answer is visually incorrect — the visually correct answer must be preferred. Workers must prioritize visual fidelity over domain plausibility — even if a claim is ‘more common-sense’ or ‘more plausible’. It is not applicable to questions asking for literal, positional, or count-based claims — and should be avoided for yes/no or binary questions unless visual evidence is unambiguous. Examples of valid applications: ‘The hydrant is silver because it is made of metal’ (material plausibility) or ‘The person is likely a skater’ (contextual logic — based on visible posture and environment). Examples of invalid applications: ‘There is a giraffe in the image’ (visually unsupported) or ‘The person is wearing a team jersey’ (visually unsupported). Workers must not use this criterion to penalize visually correct answers for being ‘less plausible’ or ‘less common-sense’ — and must not apply it to hallucinated or speculative claims — even if plausible. The criterion is not a gatekeeper — it is only a tiebreaker when visual fidelity is equal, and only for grounded, minimally speculative inferences. The description must explicitly state that this criterion is never applied to visually misrepresentative claims — even if they are domain-plausible — and that visual grounding is the sole gatekeeper. Workers must not use domain knowledge to validate or override visual facts — even if the inference is common-sense. The criterion is not about style or tone — only about logical coherence with domain knowledge — and should be applied conservatively, only when visual evidence clearly supports a minimally speculative inference. This criterion is only applicable to non-visual inferences — not to visual misrepresentations — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation if visual evidence is misrepresented or omitted. It is not a tool to penalize or validate domain plausibility in visually incorrect answers — and must be applied only to non-literal, contextually grounded inferences — not to visual facts or misrepresentations. Workers must verify each claim’s visual grounding independently — and must not rely on external assumptions or domain knowledge to validate visually incorrect claims. Any answer that misrepresents visual evidence — even if domain-plausible — is disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image — and cannot be assessed under this criterion. The criterion must be applied only to non-literal, inferential, or contextual questions — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for literal visual inventories, count-based, or positional questions — even if the inference is domain-plausible. Workers must not penalize plausible, minimally speculative inferences — even if they are not explicitly visible — as long as they are grounded in visual context and do not hallucinate. The criterion should explicitly define ‘hallucination’ as inventing visual content not present in the image — not as making plausible interpretations of visual context. It should also explicitly exclude inferences about environment or background — if those inferences are visually supported — and must not penalize such inferences as ‘unsupported’ unless they contradict visual evidence. Finally, the criterion must emphasize that it applies only to non-visual inferences — not to visual detail, positional specificity, or descriptive depth — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for aesthetic, interpretive, or stylistic descriptions — even if they are visually grounded. The criterion must be rewritten to explicitly include aesthetic and interpretive claims as valid under this criterion if they are visually grounded and domain-plausible — not excluded. It should clarify that 'domain knowledge' includes visual aesthetics, composition, and artistic function — not just material or contextual logic. The criterion must be reworded to avoid penalizing aesthetic reasoning — and should explicitly state that it is not a tool to favor 'technical' over 'aesthetic' claims — but to evaluate logical coherence with visual evidence. The criterion should also be clarified to include visual aesthetics as part of domain knowledge — and should not exclude claims about artistic function, visual harmony, or compositional intent — as long as they are grounded in visual evidence. Finally, it should be explicitly stated that this criterion is not for resolving ties between aesthetic claims — but for evaluating whether such claims are logically coherent with visual evidence — not for penalizing them as 'less grounded'.

current_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s claims are strictly grounded in visually verifiable, measurable, and unambiguous content from the image — without inventing, misrepresenting, or omitting elements that are materially relevant to the question’s literal intent. It applies ONLY to questions that explicitly demand literal visual facts — such as object identification, spatial positioning, attribute states, or counts — and is INAPPLICABLE to interpretive, aesthetic, compositional, or stylistic questions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘style’, ‘intent’, ‘how is this arranged?’, ‘what is the relationship?’, ‘describe the composition’, ‘what is the artist’s intent?’), which are evaluated under other criteria. Workers must evaluate every claim against direct visual evidence — not external knowledge, assumptions, or inferential context — and must visually inspect and confirm each claim (including text, logos, colors, textures, and spatial relationships) with absolute precision. Hallucinations — defined as inventing visual content not present (e.g., objects, text, colors, spatial relationships, or misattributed elements) — are disqualifying errors and must be penalized equally, regardless of plausibility. If visual evidence is unambiguous, no uncertainty is allowed — even if the claim is inferential or contextually grounded. If visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded, the answer must reflect uncertainty (e.g., 'appears to be', 'likely', 'based on visual evidence') — not invent details. Omitting non-critical details is acceptable — but omitting visually present, materially relevant elements (e.g., objects, text, spatial anchors) is a factual error. Claims about object mounting, structural attachment, or functional attributes must be directly verifiable — not inferred. Spatial claims (e.g., 'centered', 'near the edge', 'above', 'straight', 'curved', 'consistent spacing') must be evaluated using frame boundaries, area proportions, and relative positioning — not subjective interpretation — and must be verified independently: 'consistent spacing' is a factual claim requiring visual verification, not an inference about organizational pattern. Misidentifications (e.g., mistaking a horse for a donkey) are hallucinations if they misrepresent visual evidence — and must be penalized. All claims must be anchored to concrete, measurable visual evidence — not abstract or inferential descriptions. The criterion does NOT apply to: (1) stylistic, contextual, or domain-specific interpretations — those are evaluated under ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’; (2) questions asking for artist attribution, title, provenance, or external factual claims — unless those claims are visually verifiable (e.g., visible signature, title on canvas); (3) questions requiring inferential, causal, or behavioral analysis — even if grounded in visual context — unless explicitly asking for literal, measurable facts; (4) questions asking for operating systems or software — which are evaluated based on UI elements, icons, or layout — not brand logos; (5) questions asking for ‘thorough descriptions’, ‘detailed text inclusion’, or ‘character analysis’ — which are inherently interpretive and evaluated under ‘completeness’ or ‘specificity’; (6) questions involving metaphorical, symbolic, or interpretive visual content — which are evaluated under ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’. If visual evidence contradicts external knowledge, the visual evidence must prevail — even if it is counterintuitive. Workers must not penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations. The answer must not rely on context, branding, or brand association to make claims about visual content — only direct visual evidence. Text, logos, and visible attributes (e.g., 'Coca-Cola' text, red color, 'Answers' label) must be verified visually — not assumed or inferred. Claims about operating systems or software must be verifiable via UI elements, icons, or layout — not brand logos. All claims must be grounded in visual plausibility — not abstract reasoning. If visual evidence is insufficient to confirm or deny a claim, the answer must reflect uncertainty — not make speculative assertions. If both answers are factually consistent, the more complete or accurate visual description is preferred — but never at the cost of introducing hallucinations. The criterion does NOT apply to questions asking for hypothetical, biological, or non-visual interpretations — those are evaluated under other criteria. If a claim is visually verifiable — even if negative or partial — it is factually consistent. Absolute denials (e.g., 'no one is wearing jerseys') must be verified — and if false, they are penalized — but if true, they are not. All hallucinations are equally disqualifying — no severity ranking is allowed. Workers must trust the image over assumptions, even if the image is ambiguous or misinterpreted. If visual evidence is clear, any misrepresentation is a hallucination — regardless of how plausible it may seem. If both answers contain hallucinations, mark both as incorrect — or if forced to choose, the answer with fewer hallucinations is preferred — but only after verifying that the hallucinations are clearly distinguishable. The criterion must be applied consistently — no subjective error classification is allowed — only strict visual verification for all claims. It is not a tiebreaker — it is a gatekeeper: if an answer contains a hallucination, it is disqualified — and factual consistency is the only criterion that can validate an answer for tiebreaker evaluation. Workers must NOT apply this criterion to questions that are not explicitly literal, measurable, or inventory-style — even if the answer contains some visual grounding — and must defer to other criteria (e.g., ‘specificity’, ‘completeness’, ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’) for interpretive, compositional, or relational questions. If visual evidence is insufficient or ambiguous — and the question is not explicitly literal — workers must mark the answer as uncertain — and must not apply this criterion. The criterion must not penalize reasonable, contextually grounded inferences — as long as they do not invent non-existent visual content — and must not penalize omission of non-critical details — as long as those details are not materially relevant to the question’s intent. Finally, the criterion must explicitly exclude static, stylized, or non-living visual content — such as statues — from hallucination penalties if they accurately reflect visually verifiable attributes (e.g., bent legs) — even if those attributes are non-biological or stylized — and must not penalize descriptions of visual form for being 'too specific' or 'potentially misleading' — only if they misrepresent or invent visual content.

current_criteria.name: logical_coherence_of_visual_sequence
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s visual claims form a logically consistent, temporally or causally progressive sequence — applicable ONLY when the question explicitly and unambiguously demands a multi-step, sequential, or transformational visual reasoning task (e.g., ‘what happened next?’, ‘how does this unfold?’, ‘what is the progression?’). It is inapplicable to all other question types — including static images, single-event identification, descriptive composition, inventory-style questions, spatial relationships (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘to the left of’), aesthetic or stylistic descriptions, and any question not explicitly requesting visual event progression. The criterion is a strict gatekeeper: if the question does not explicitly demand sequence, this criterion is inapplicable — and preference must be based solely on visual grounding and factual consistency (under factual_consistency_with_the_image). It is NEVER a tiebreaker for non-sequential questions — and must never override or substitute for factual_consistency_with_the_image. Workers must evaluate applicability first — and if the question is not sequential, they must defer to other criteria — without applying this criterion. This criterion evaluates only factually correct, visually grounded answers — and if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from this criterion — regardless of sequence. It does NOT penalize factually correct answers for including unsupported inferences — only for unsupported inferences in factually correct answers — and must not be used to penalize factually correct answers for being ‘less sequential’ or ‘less coherent’ in a non-sequential context. ‘Unsupported’ refers exclusively to hallucinations — not to verifiable but non-essential details — and must not penalize factually correct answers for including visually verifiable details — even if they are not required by the question — or for including ‘unnecessary detail’ unless it is a hallucination. The criterion is never a tool to prefer simpler or less detailed answers — and must be applied only to questions that explicitly demand sequence — with no fallback to other criteria. It is NOT a tool to resolve ties between factually incorrect answers — which must be disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image — and must not be applied to factually incorrect answers — even if the question involves sequence — or to any answer that is factually incorrect — even if it appears more sequential. ‘Sequence’ refers strictly to temporal or causal progression — not spatial or compositional relationships — and must avoid any implication that visual descriptions, text-based answers, or compositional claims can be evaluated under this criterion. Workers must not assume temporal or causal progression from static visual context — and must not apply this criterion to questions that do not explicitly demand a sequence. Logical coherence is evaluated solely for visual sequences involving temporal progression or causal transitions — not for narrative structure, spatial organization, or compositional flow. Examples of applicability: ‘The person walks to the door, opens it, and steps outside’ — each action must be visually grounded and temporally coherent. Examples of inapplicability: ‘What is on the screen?’ — static inventory; ‘Describe the composition’ — static arrangement; ‘What software is this?’ — single-event identification; ‘What is the mood?’ — inferential, non-sequential; ‘The red car is to the left of the tree’ — spatial, not sequential. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy — and logical coherence is irrelevant for non-sequential questions — which must be resolved under other criteria — including factual_consistency_with_the_image. The criterion must be applied conservatively — and must not be used to penalize or reward non-sequential answers — even if they appear logically coherent — and must not be misinterpreted as a tiebreaker for factually incorrect answers — which must be disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image.

current_criteria.name: robustness_to_visual_noise
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer remains valid or is appropriately qualified under measurable visual degradation — such as blur, compression artifacts, occlusion, or low resolution — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresentations. It is ONLY applicable when: (1) the image explicitly contains or simulates measurable visual degradation that challenges the verifiability of literal visual claims (e.g., identifying an object, reading text, or detecting color under noise), and (2) the question explicitly demands a literal, measurable visual claim (e.g., ‘what is the text?’, ‘what color is the object?’, ‘what is on the table?’). If either condition is not met, the criterion is inapplicable — and workers must defer to other criteria (e.g., factual_consistency_with_the_image, visual grounding, specificity) for preference judgment. The answer must either correctly identify the visual element despite degradation — or qualify its claim with uncertainty markers (e.g., ‘appears to be’, ‘likely’, ‘based on degraded visual evidence’) — without inventing details not supported by the degraded visual context. Hallucinations — defined as inventing non-existent visual content — are always disqualifying under factual_consistency_with_the_image — and this criterion is not applied to hallucinated or factually incorrect answers — even if they appear ‘noise-resistant’ or ‘stable’. This criterion is a tiebreaker ONLY when both answers are factually correct, visually grounded, and both involve the same type of visual degradation — and only for literal visual claims. Workers must NOT penalize factually correct answers for being less cautious or less specific — only for hallucinations or misrepresentations that arise from degradation. The criterion does NOT evaluate specificity, detail level, linguistic precision, or aesthetic interpretations — and must not be used to resolve ties between factually correct answers. Robustness to noise is not a substitute for factual accuracy — and must be applied only after verifying factual consistency and visual grounding — and must never override or substitute for factual accuracy. The criterion must be explicitly gated by the presence of measurable visual degradation — and must be skipped entirely if the image is clear, unambiguous, or if the question does not involve degradation. Workers must not confuse visual noise with visual ambiguity or inferential plausibility — and must evaluate only whether claims withstand degradation — not whether they are more ‘cautious’ or ‘minimalist’. Uncertainty markers are allowed — but only when visual evidence is degraded — and must not be used to hedge claims that are factually correct in clear images. The criterion must explicitly exclude stylized, labeled, or childlike visual content — which are not evaluated under this criterion — and must not penalize accurate, contextually grounded descriptions — even if they are not ‘noise-resistant’. Visual grounding is a prerequisite — and robustness is irrelevant if the visual claim is false or hallucinated. The criterion is not a tool to penalize vagueness — only to penalize hallucinations — and must be applied conservatively — to avoid penalizing grounded, contextually necessary interpretations — even in degraded images. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy — and robustness to noise is only a secondary metric for evaluating claims that are factually correct under degradation. The criterion must be applied only to literal visual identification or attribute extraction tasks — not to descriptive, aesthetic, or compositional questions — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for questions that are not explicitly about visual degradation. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that it does not apply to questions where visual evidence is simply not present or ambiguous due to the scene’s nature — not due to noise — and must require that the visual noise be a measurable, inherent, or simulated variable — not a contextual or semantic gap.

current_criteria.name: specificity
current_criteria.description: Specificity evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer includes only minimally necessary, measurably precise, and directly verifiable visual attributes that directly fulfill the question’s explicit demand for quantifiable visual precision — such as exact counts, spatial coordinates, color, size, text content, or attribute states — and is ONLY applicable when the question explicitly requires such precision (e.g., ‘how many?’, ‘what color?’, ‘where is it?’, ‘what text?’, ‘what is the exact position?’). It is inapplicable to all questions that are interpretive, aesthetic, compositional, inferential, contextual, narrative, or metaphorical — even if visually grounded — and to questions where visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded — in which case the answer must reflect uncertainty (e.g., ‘appears to be’, ‘likely’, ‘based on visual evidence’). Specificity is a tiebreaker metric ONLY when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and only for questions that explicitly demand measurable visual attributes — and must not be applied to questions that are inherently inventory-style, descriptive, or contextual — even if they involve visual positioning — which are evaluated under completeness or visual grounding. It does NOT penalize contextually necessary, minimally inferential phrases (e.g., ‘above the Ctrl key’, ‘in the foreground’, ‘small portion’, ‘most of the space’) as long as they are visually verifiable and not hallucinated — and must NOT be used to penalize factually correct, contextually rich answers for being less quantitative — especially when the question’s intent is not measurable. Specificity rewards grounded precision — not verbosity, irrelevant detail, or speculative claims — and includes multi-element descriptions (e.g., ‘the red car is left of the tree, behind the fence’) as long as all elements are visually verifiable and non-hallucinatory. It does not apply to linguistic, semantic, or abstract factual claims (e.g., brand names, software inferences) unless directly verifiable via visual attributes (e.g., ‘the logo is red’ or ‘the text says ‘macOS’’). Workers must verify that the answer is factually correct and visually grounded — and if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from specificity evaluation — regardless of precision. Specificity is NOT a gatekeeper or primary metric — it is only a tiebreaker — and must never override factual accuracy or visual grounding. Hallucinations (inventing visual content not present) are disqualifying under factual_consistency_with_the_image — and specificity is not applied to hallucinated answers — even if they are minimally specific. Workers must NOT apply specificity to questions that are inherently interpretive, compositional, or aesthetic — even if they involve visual positioning — and must explicitly exclude such questions from evaluation. The criterion must explicitly state that ‘measurable’ refers to quantifiable visual attributes — not qualitative descriptions of visual arrangement (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’, ‘harmonious’), and must define ‘measurable’ as including counts, exact spatial positions, color, size, text, or text content — not spatial relationships, visual hierarchy, or compositional intent. Workers must prioritize visual grounding and factual consistency — and any answer with factual errors or visual misrepresentations is disqualified — regardless of specificity. Specificity is NOT applicable to binary, yes/no, or simple factual questions — which are evaluated under other criteria. It does NOT penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations — and must not be used to penalize factually correct, contextually rich answers for being ‘less literal’. Workers must not infer measurable precision from questions that are inherently interpretive — and must explicitly exclude all questions asking for ‘in-depth description’, ‘character analysis’, ‘thorough description’, or ‘include text contents’ — as these are inherently inventory-style or contextual — and should be evaluated under completeness or visual grounding. The criterion must explicitly state that it is only evaluated for questions that explicitly demand measurable visual attributes — and must be skipped entirely if the question is not explicitly measurable. Workers must NOT use specificity to resolve ties between hallucinated or factually incorrect answers — and must defer to other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency) for such cases. Specificity must be applied conservatively — and must never override or substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that ‘measurable’ includes relative, contextual, or comparative visual attributes — not only exact counts or positions — and must allow for grounded, contextually necessary details (e.g., ‘small portion’, ‘most of the space’) — as long as they are not hallucinated and visually supported — and must not penalize such details as long as they are factually correct and visually grounded. Additionally, it must explicitly exclude any question that does not explicitly demand measurable precision — including questions asking for ‘approximate’ or ‘relative’ positions — unless they demand a precise, measurable, and verifiable spatial anchor — and must require that any claim of precision be visually grounded, not linguistically optimized. It must also penalize answers that use speculative or non-verifiable anatomical terms — even if they appear 'more specific' — and must be applied only to questions that explicitly demand verifiable, measurable, and directly observable visual attributes — not to questions asking for approximate or relative positions. Workers must prioritize visual verifiability over linguistic specificity — and must not apply specificity to questions that are inferential, contextual, or require explanation — even if visually grounded — and must gate its application strictly on questions that explicitly demand quantifiable visual attributes — such as ‘where is the object?’, ‘how many?’, ‘what color?’, ‘what text?’, or ‘what is the exact position?’. It must also explicitly exclude questions asking about positioning or composition as inapplicable — since these are inherently interpretive and aesthetic, not measurable visual precision demands — and must not penalize contextually grounded inferences — only hallucinations. The criterion must be applied only after verifying factual accuracy — and must not be used to penalize factually correct answers for being less quantitative — especially when the question’s intent is not measurable. Workers must verify that the answer is factually correct and visually grounded — and if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from specificity evaluation — regardless of precision. Specificity is only a tiebreaker when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and only for questions that explicitly demand measurable visual attributes — with no fallback or misapplication for non-measurable questions. current_criteria.name: temporal_consistency_of_visual_elements
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s visual claims about motion, state change, or spatial evolution are temporally consistent across frames or time — applicable ONLY when the question explicitly involves sequences, multi-frame comparisons, or temporal evolution (e.g., ‘what changes between frames?’, ‘how does the object move?’, ‘what happens next?’). Workers must first verify that all claims are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — any answer with hallucinations or misrepresentations is disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image, regardless of temporal context. If both answers are factually correct and visually grounded, temporal consistency is evaluated as a tiebreaker: the answer with the more coherent, verifiable sequence of visual transitions (e.g., trajectory, motion blur, sequential positioning) is preferred. Workers must not penalize cautious phrasing, semantic drift, or vagueness — only misrepresentations of motion or state transitions not supported by visual evidence. This criterion is inapplicable to static images, questions without temporal context (e.g., ‘what is on the table?’, ‘describe the composition’, ‘what is the object’s color?’), or questions requiring inferential or metaphorical motion (e.g., ‘the scene flows’), which are evaluated under other criteria. When inapplicable, workers must still evaluate factual_consistency_with_the_image and visual grounding — and must not use inapplicability as a reason to select a less factually accurate answer. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy over temporal coherence — and must never use this criterion to override or justify selecting an answer that is factually incorrect — even if it is more temporally consistent. The criterion must be applied conservatively — and only when the question explicitly involves temporal evolution — with no tolerance for misapplication. Workers must verify all claims against the image — even in inapplicable cases — to ensure factual accuracy. Visual evidence must be verified for all claims — not just temporal ones — and workers must not confuse temporal evolution with literal motion or state change — e.g., spatial progression (e.g., rising water levels) qualifies as temporal evolution if explicitly demanded. Finally, workers must not assume an answer is correct based on temporal coherence alone — and must always evaluate for hallucinations, misrepresentations, or factual errors — even if the criterion is inapplicable. The criterion is explicitly gated by the requirement that the question must explicitly demand temporal evolution — and must not be used to evaluate or resolve ties involving hallucinated, factually incorrect, or visually ungrounded answers — even if the question is about motion or sequence. Workers must never apply this criterion to static or non-temporal questions — even if one answer is more contextually grounded or specific — and must defer to other criteria (e.g., specificity, visual grounding, completeness) for preference when the criterion is inapplicable. The criterion is not a tiebreaker for factual accuracy — only for temporal coherence — and must not be used to validate or override factual correctness. Workers must not confuse spatial arrangement, compositional detail, or aesthetic interpretation with temporal evolution — and must strictly adhere to the requirement that the question explicitly involve motion, state change, or sequence — even if visual evidence is static — to qualify for this criterion. The description must explicitly state that temporal_consistency is never a fallback or substitute for factual_consistency_with_the_image — and that the worker must always evaluate for hallucinations, misrepresentations, or factual errors — even if the question is static or the criterion is inapplicable. current_criteria.name: visual_stability_under_transformation
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer’s claims about color, shape, material, or text content remain visually verifiable and stable under minor, realistic image transformations — such as rotation, zoom, cropping, or color shift — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresentations. It is ONLY applicable when the answer explicitly makes a claim about one of these invariant visual properties (e.g., ‘the dress is black’, ‘the lips are red’, ‘the text says ‘macOS’’, ‘the object is circular’) — and the claim must be objectively unchanged under the transformation (i.e., the visual property remains true even if rotated, zoomed, or cropped — assuming visual content is preserved). The answer must first be verified as factually correct and visually grounded — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from this criterion. This criterion is NOT a tiebreaker — it is used solely as a secondary validation for claims about invariant visual properties — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for any question or answer that does not involve such a claim. It is not a substitute for factual accuracy — and must not override visual grounding or factual consistency. Workers must evaluate only claims that are objectively invariant under transformation — not subjective interpretations, contextual claims, spatial relationships, aesthetic descriptions, or inferential inferences (e.g., ‘on the left’, ‘mood’, ‘human-shaped’, ‘browsing Apple pages’, ‘in the background’, ‘modern feel’, ‘abstract style’). Workers must strictly adhere to this exclusion list — and if any condition is violated, the criterion is not applied — and the worker must defer to other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency, specificity, completeness) for preference judgment. This criterion should be applied conservatively — and only when the answer makes a claim about color, shape, material, or text content — with no fallback or tiebreaker function. Workers must NOT use this criterion to penalize factually correct answers for being ‘less stable’ — and must not apply it to questions that are not visual in nature — or to questions that do not involve invariant property claims. The criterion is designed to identify and penalize hallucinations or misrepresentations that become false under transformation — not to evaluate the quality of contextual or spatial descriptions — even if those descriptions are factually correct. Workers must not confuse ‘invariant properties’ with ‘presence/absence’ or ‘binary claims’ — and must always defer to visual evidence for factual correctness when the criterion is inapplicable. It should also clarify that stability under transformation is not a tool to override factual accuracy — and must be applied only after verifying factual correctness. Additionally, it should emphasize that the criterion is not a tiebreaker — and must not be used to evaluate answers that are factually incorrect — even if they are stable under transformation. If the answer is factually incorrect — e.g., claiming ‘the text says ‘Windows’’ — it is disqualified from all criteria — even if the text claim is stable under transformation — because factual correctness is a mandatory prerequisite.

current_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty_in_contextual_questions
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer appropriately expresses uncertainty when the question involves subjective, inferential, or contextually ambiguous visual interpretation — without over- or under-qualifying. It is applicable ONLY when the question demands interpretation, inference, or contextual reasoning (e.g., ‘what is the mood?’, ‘how does this feel?’, ‘what might be happening?’), and the visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or requires non-literal inference. The answer must use calibrated uncertainty markers (e.g., ‘likely’, ‘appears to be’, ‘based on visual cues’, ‘possibly’, ‘it seems like’) without overgeneralizing (e.g., ‘definitely’, ‘always’, ‘clearly’) or under-qualifying (e.g., ‘it’s this’, ‘it’s that’) — and must avoid definitive claims when evidence is ambiguous. It is a tiebreaker only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and only for questions where uncertainty is contextually warranted. This criterion is inapplicable to literal, measurable, or inventory-style questions — which are evaluated under other criteria — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for questions with clear, unambiguous visual evidence. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy — and this criterion must not override visual grounding or factual consistency. It does NOT penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations or overconfidence in ambiguous contexts. The criterion must be applied conservatively — and must not be used to penalize factually correct answers for being ‘less certain’ — only for inappropriate or excessive uncertainty markers. Workers must verify that the answer is factually correct and visually grounded — and if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from this criterion — regardless of uncertainty expression. The criterion is not a substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency — and must be evaluated only after those are confirmed. It is not applicable to questions asking for literal, measurable, or compositional answers — and must defer to other criteria for such cases. The description must include a clear example: for a question ‘what is the mood?’, an answer ‘somber, likely due to the dim lighting’ is appropriate — while ‘dark and somber’ without justification is overconfident and penalized — and ‘it’s hard to say’ without context is under-qualified. The criterion must explicitly state that it is only applicable to questions where uncertainty is contextually warranted — and must not be used to penalize factually correct answers for being ‘too vague’. It must also clarify that ‘calibrated uncertainty’ means using appropriate, context-sensitive language — not just adding ‘maybe’ or ‘perhaps’ — and must avoid penalizing answers that are factually correct for being less specific. Finally, it must emphasize that this criterion is not a tiebreaker — and must not be applied to factually incorrect answers — even if they appear more uncertain. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy — and uncertainty is only a tool to express epistemic limitation — not a substitute for correctness.

all_criteria.name: visual_grounding
all_criteria.description: The answer must accurately reflect what is visible in the image — describing objects, positions, colors, textures, and actions as they appear. It should not invent or misrepresent visual elements. Evaluated by direct comparison to the image content.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question asked, without drifting into irrelevant topics or tangential information. Evaluated by whether the answer’s core focus aligns with the question’s intent.

all_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
all_criteria.description: The answer must strictly align with visually verifiable content in the image — including object identities, locations, states, counts, and spatial relationships — without misrepresenting, inventing, or omitting critical visual evidence that is materially relevant to the question’s intent. Hallucinations (invented objects, misidentified attributes, misattributed elements, or false claims about non-existent visual content) are disqualifying errors — regardless of plausibility — and must be penalized equally, without severity ranking. If visual evidence is unambiguous, no uncertainty is allowed — even if the claim is speculative or inferential. If visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded, the answer must reflect uncertainty (e.g., 'appears to be', 'likely', 'based on visual evidence') — not invent details. Omitting non-critical details is acceptable — but omitting visually present, materially relevant elements (e.g., objects, text, spatial anchors) is a factual error. Claims about object mounting, structural attachment, or functional attributes must be directly verifiable — not inferred. Spatial claims (e.g., 'centered', 'near the edge', 'above', 'straight', 'curved', 'consistent spacing') must be evaluated using frame boundaries, area proportions, and relative positioning — not subjective interpretation — and must be verified independently: 'consistent spacing' is a factual claim requiring visual verification, not an inference about organizational pattern. Misidentifications (e.g., mistaking a horse for a donkey) are hallucinations if they misrepresent visual evidence — and must be penalized. All claims must be anchored to concrete, measurable visual evidence — not abstract or inferential descriptions. The criterion does not apply to stylistic, contextual, or domain-specific interpretations — those are evaluated under ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’. If visual evidence contradicts external knowledge, the visual evidence must prevail — even if it is counterintuitive. Workers must not penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations. The answer must not rely on context, branding, or brand association to make claims about visual content — only direct visual evidence. Text, logos, and visible attributes (e.g., 'Coca-Cola' text, red color, 'Answers' label) must be verified visually — not assumed or inferred. Claims about operating systems or software must be verifiable via UI elements, icons, or layout — not brand logos. All claims must be grounded in visual plausibility — not abstract reasoning. If visual evidence is insufficient to confirm or deny a claim, the answer must reflect uncertainty — not make speculative assertions. If both answers are factually consistent, the more complete or accurate visual description is preferred — but never at the cost of introducing hallucinations. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for hypothetical, biological, or non-visual interpretations — those are evaluated under other criteria. If a claim is visually verifiable — even if negative or partial — it is factually consistent. Absolute denials (e.g., 'no one is wearing jerseys') must be verified — and if false, they are penalized — but if true, they are not. All hallucinations are equally disqualifying — no severity ranking is allowed. Workers must trust the image over assumptions, even if the image is ambiguous or misinterpreted. If visual evidence is clear, any misrepresentation is a hallucination — regardless of how plausible it may seem. If both answers contain hallucinations, mark both as incorrect — or if forced to choose, the answer with fewer hallucinations is preferred — but only after verifying that the hallucinations are clearly distinguishable. The criterion does not apply to external factual claims (e.g., artist attribution, title, provenance) unless those claims are visually verifiable (e.g., visible signature, title on canvas). Workers should evaluate only claims directly observable in the image — not external metadata. If the question asks for a description of the image’s content, the answer may include contextual facts — but if not visually present, they are not required and should not be penalized for omission. Visual descriptions (e.g., color, object type) are evaluated based on visual plausibility and context — not strict technical terminology. If multiple object labels are visually plausible (e.g., 'jet ski' vs 'water scooter'), the answer that is more visually accurate in composition, positioning, and color should be preferred — even if it uses a less precise term. Object identification errors are disqualifying, but color or spatial description errors are only penalized if they are clearly false or hallucinated — and visual composition and spatial relationships should be prioritized over precise terminology. Spatial relationships must be evaluated based on visual perspective — not subjective interpretation. Hallucinations include misplacement of objects, misattribution of visual elements, and false claims about non-existent visual content. All claims must be visually grounded — even if the visual evidence is partially obscured or low-resolution — and workers must not assume or infer visual content. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., whether needles are 'icy' or 'cold'), the answer must reflect uncertainty — but if the visual evidence is unambiguous, no such ambiguity exists, and any misrepresentation must be rejected. If a claim is visually unsupported (e.g., 'half-squatting'), it must be marked as such or avoided — not assumed. Visual grounding and factual consistency are interdependent — and ambiguity or inference must be clearly qualified — not assumed. All claims must be verified — regardless of their type. If both answers are factually inconsistent, the one with fewer unsupported claims (even if more severe) should be selected — or both should be marked incorrect — but never that a misidentification is 'less' inconsistent than a hallucination if both are visually unsupported. The criterion must be applied consistently — no subjective error classification is allowed — only strict visual verification for all claims.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucinated_visual_details

all_criteria.name: completeness
all_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether a visually grounded and factually correct answer includes all semantically required visual elements necessary to fulfill the question’s literal, measurable visual inventory demand — and only when the question explicitly demands a multi-element, inventory-style response (e.g., ‘list all objects’, ‘what is on the table?’, ‘describe composition’, ‘what is the text?’). It is inapplicable to: (1) binary, yes/no, or single-attribute questions (e.g., ‘Is this a red car?’), (2) interpretive, inferential, or contextual questions (e.g., ‘What is the mood?’, ‘What is the object doing?’, ‘Describe the style’), (3) questions requiring inferred action, behavior, or state — even if visual objects are present — because those are not inventory-style, (4) aesthetic or compositional questions asking about framing, contrast, or structure — unless explicitly demanding a literal visual inventory (e.g., ‘list all foreground/background elements’), (5) questions where visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — in which case the answer must reflect calibrated uncertainty or question relevance, and (6) any question that does not explicitly demand an exhaustive, individualized visual inventory (e.g., general, representative, or averaged descriptions). Completeness is only a tiebreaker metric — and only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — comparing which answer includes all semantically required visual elements (e.g., visible objects, text, logos, spatial relationships, compositional framing) without omission. Completeness does not reward verbosity — but penalizes omission of semantically required elements — even if the answer includes non-essential commentary. It is not a standalone metric — and should never override factual accuracy or visual grounding. Workers must evaluate only visually verifiable elements — not inferential or conceptual interpretations — and must reject any answer that misrepresents visual evidence — even if it appears thorough. When visual evidence is ambiguous, completeness is not evaluated — and workers must mark the answer as uncertain. Examples of applicability: ‘What is on the table?’ → list all visible items on the table; ‘What is the color of the text?’ → include all visible text colors; ‘Describe the composition’ → include foreground/background, spatial relationships, and framing. Examples of inapplicability: ‘What is the mood?’ → interpretive, not visual inventory; ‘What is the object doing?’ → inferential, not direct visual inventory; ‘Is this a red car?’ → binary, not multi-element; ‘What is the object’s function?’ → inferential, not visual. Completeness must be evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and if an answer contains a factual error, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of coverage. Workers must not use completeness to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must prioritize factual coverage over stylistic minimalism. Completeness is not applicable to questions where the answer is a single factual claim — even if it involves inference — and must be evaluated only for multi-element, inventory-style questions with clear, unambiguous visual evidence. Workers must not apply completeness to hallucinated or visually unsupported claims — even if plausible — and must not penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — only for omission of semantically required elements. The criterion is not a tool to resolve ties between visually incorrect or hallucinated answers — only between factually correct, visually grounded answers. The description must unambiguously exclude any question type not meeting the above criteria — including subjective, inferential, or ambiguous questions — and must explicitly state that completeness is only a tiebreaker for inventory-style questions with clear visual evidence. Workers must not assume that all visible visual elements are ‘semantically relevant’ — only those directly required to answer the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also avoid penalizing factual, verifiable details that are visually present and directly relevant to the question’s literal intent — even if they are not the ‘primary’ answer. The description must clearly state that for binary classification or posture-based questions, the visual distinction (e.g., ‘legs bent’) is semantically required — and that omission of such a detail, even if not the ‘main point’, reduces completeness. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that ‘unnecessary detail’ refers to non-essential, contextually irrelevant information — not factual, visually verifiable details that are critical to answering the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also explicitly state that completeness does not apply to questions requiring inferred action, behavior, or state — even if visual objects are present — because those are not inventory-style. It must also clarify that 'semantically required' elements are those necessary to fulfill the question’s literal, measurable, or compositional intent — not speculative or exaggerated claims about dominance, proportion, or scale. It must also prohibit penalizing answers for omitting such claims if they are visually ambiguous or not essential to the question’s intent — and must explicitly exclude compositional or relational questions from being evaluated under completeness unless they demand explicit, verifiable quantitative or spatial comparisons. Additionally, the criterion should explicitly warn workers not to confuse completeness with precision or verbosity — and to avoid penalizing factually correct answers for being less detailed — especially when the added detail is unsupported or misleading. The criterion must be applied only when the question explicitly demands a multi-element, inventory-style visual description — and must not be applied to open-ended, detail-rich, or subjective questions. It must also clarify that completeness rewards inclusion of semantically required visual elements — not any visible details — and must penalize omission of those elements — even if the answer includes other non-essential details. The criterion must also explicitly exclude questions that are not inventory-style — and must require that the question’s intent be unambiguous — to avoid misapplication. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that completeness is not a tiebreaker — and must not be used to penalize answers for being less detailed — only for omitting semantically required elements. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy — and completeness is only a tiebreaker for factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must not be applied to factually incorrect answers — even if they appear more complete.
